blocks.content: This closing topic of the HTTP and HTTPS module traces how HTTP itself has evolved over time, from HTTP 1.1, still genuinely common today, through HTTP 2, to HTTP 3, the newest version, built on a fundamentally different transport foundation entirely. Each version fixes a real, honest limitation of the one before it.

Everything covered elsewhere in this module, methods, status codes, the request response model itself, stays conceptually the same across all these versions. What actually changes is the underlying mechanics of how requests and responses are physically carried across the connection.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437777779-524071058.png
1. HTTP 1.1: The Long Standing Baseline

HTTP 1.1 has a real, honest limitation: on a single connection, one request generally has to fully finish before the next one can begin. Loading a page with many separate resources, images, scripts, stylesheets, means either waiting for them one at a time on one connection, or browsers opening several separate connections in parallel to work around it.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437777780-556109075.png
2. Head of Line Blocking, the Core HTTP 1.1 Problem
blocks.text: 2. Head of Line Blocking, the Core HTTP 1.1 Problem

blocks.content: This specific limitation has a real name, head of line blocking. If request 1 on a connection is slow, requests 2 and 3 queued up behind it on that exact same connection are forced to wait, even though they are completely unrelated and would otherwise be perfectly ready to proceed immediately.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437777781-830400927.png
blocks.alt: Head of Line Blocking, the Core HTTP 1.1 Problem

blocks.content: 3. HTTP 2: Multiplexing Fixes This at the HTTP Level
blocks.text: 3. HTTP 2: Multiplexing Fixes This at the HTTP Level

blocks.content: HTTP 2 introduces multiplexing, letting many requests and responses be interleaved freely over a single connection at once. A slow request no longer blocks unrelated ones sharing that same connection, genuinely solving the head of line blocking problem, at least at the HTTP protocol level itself.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437777781-208211116.png
blocks.alt: HTTP 2: Multiplexing Fixes This at the HTTP Level

4. Other Genuine HTTP 2 Improvements

Beyond multiplexing, HTTP 2 also introduced header compression, reducing the real, repeated overhead of sending largely similar headers on every single request, and server push, letting a server proactively send resources it already knows a client will need, before the client even explicitly asks for them.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437777781-607314167.png
5. The Limitation HTTP 2 Could Not Fully Fix
blocks.text: 5. The Limitation HTTP 2 Could Not Fully Fix

blocks.content: HTTP 2 fixed head of line blocking at the HTTP protocol level, but it still runs over an ordinary TCP connection underneath, exactly the reliable, strictly ordered delivery covered in the reliability-in-tcp topic. Since TCP itself delivers all data on a connection strictly in order, a single lost TCP segment can still stall literally everything else behind it on that connection, even unrelated HTTP streams, an honest limitation HTTP 2 alone genuinely could not solve.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437777781-302599536.png
blocks.alt: The Limitation HTTP 2 Could Not Fully Fix

blocks.title: A genuinely subtle, important distinction
blocks.content: This is exactly why head of line blocking, seemingly solved by HTTP 2, can still show up in practice, the problem simply moved down one layer, from the HTTP protocol itself to the TCP connection carrying it.
6. HTTP 3: A New Foundation Entirely

HTTP 3 solves this remaining limitation by changing the underlying transport itself. Rather than running over TCP, HTTP 3 is built on QUIC, which runs over UDP instead. This lets individual streams genuinely operate independently, even at the transport level itself, so a lost piece of data affecting one stream no longer stalls the others sharing the same overall connection.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437777781-378161873.png

blocks.title: A direct callback to the tcp-vs-udp topic
blocks.content: This is a genuinely interesting real world example of the tcp-vs-udp topic tradeoff in action, HTTP 3 deliberately gives up some of TCP built in guarantees in exchange for QUIC own custom reliability logic, specifically to avoid TCP strict ordering across unrelated streams.
7. The Full Comparison

Tracing the evolution together makes the improvement concrete: HTTP 1.1 is effectively sequential per connection. HTTP 2 is multiplexed at the HTTP level, but still ultimately ordered underneath by TCP. HTTP 3 is multiplexed AND genuinely independent, even down at the transport level itself, closing the remaining gap entirely.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437777782-279379656.png

8. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

items: Assuming HTTP 2 fully eliminated head of line blocking, when it only solved it at the HTTP level, the underlying TCP connection could still stall everything behind one lost segment.

Assuming a newer HTTP version changes what HTTP fundamentally does, methods, status codes, and the request response model all stay conceptually identical across every version, only the underlying mechanics change.
HTTP 1.1 generally processes one request at a time per connection, a real, honest limitation.
HTTP 2 introduced multiplexing, header compression, and server push, fixing head of line blocking at the HTTP level.
HTTP 3, built on QUIC over UDP instead of TCP, finally closes the remaining transport level gap entirely.
